document_check.note: Devlin KN, Brennan L, Saad L, Giovannetti T, Hamilton RH, Wolk DA, Xie SX, Mechanic-Hamilton D, 'Diagnosing Mild Cognitive Impairment Among Racially Diverse Older Adults: Comparison of Consensus, Actuarial, and Statistical Methods', J Alzheimers Dis 2022;85(2):627-644 (PMC author manuscript). The document reports N = 354; MCI rates of 44% (consensus), 53% (actuarial) and 41% (LCA); and the race pattern (pp. 1, 7, 8).

cited_result: Principal: the proportions of the same 354 participants classified as MCI by clinical consensus (44%), actuarial Jak/Bondi criteria (53%) and latent class analysis (41%), meaning the definitions diverge in prevalence. Also cited: Black participants were less often classified MCI than White participants by consensus and LCA but equally often by actuarial criteria (N = 343).
tool_reason: The principal cited result is a set of proportions classified as MCI under three definitions in one sample, which is a prevalence-type estimate. The secondary race comparison is a one-time-point association and is discussed in the notes.

domains.domain: Item 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.rationale: The sample is a convenience cohort from a memory-centre research core, not a population frame. The absolute rates therefore do not estimate prevalence in any defined population, although within-sample comparison across definitions is still informative.

signalling.question: Was the sample frame appropriate to address the target population?
signalling.quote: Participants were enrolled through a combination of clinician referral, self-referral, and community recruitment. They included individuals presenting with memory concerns and those interested in participating in research as healthy volunteers.

domains.rationale: Sampling was not random or consecutive. Inclusion required complete data on all 14 tests and a consensus diagnosis of NC or MCI, so one of the compared definitions also defines the sample boundary. The authors acknowledge selection bias.

signalling.question: Were study participants sampled in an appropriate way?
signalling.quote: Inclusion criteria for the present study were 1) complete data for all 14 cognitive measures of interest (see below) at one or more visits, the earliest of which was classified as the baseline visit; 2) age 55 or older at baseline; 3) English as primary language; and 4) clinical consensus diagnosis of normal cognition (NC) or MCI at baseline. / Clinic-based samples are susceptible to selection bias

domains.rationale: No sample-size or precision calculation is reported, and no confidence intervals are given for the proportions.

signalling.question: Was the sample size adequate?
signalling.quote: Searched for a sample-size calculation, power analysis or confidence intervals for the rates. The only related statement is: 'Cognitive domain scores, rather than individual test scores, were entered as indicators in LCA to ensure sufficient statistical power.'

domains.domain: Item 4. Subjects and setting described in detail
domains.rationale: The setting, age range, race, education and literacy are reported.

signalling.question: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
signalling.quote: Participants ranged in age from 55–93. Most participants identified as White (68%), and Black participants were well represented (29%), but other racial and ethnic groups were not.

domains.domain: Item 5. Sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.rationale: Complete data were an inclusion criterion, so all 354 participants were classified by all three methods. The race analyses were restricted to White and Black participants (N = 343).

signalling.question: Was the data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample?
signalling.quote: Black participants were less likely than White participants to be diagnosed with MCI by consensus [27% versus 51%; χ2 (1, N = 343) = 16.18, p < 0.001]

domains.domain: Item 6. Valid methods for identification of the condition
domains.rationale: Each definition follows a published operationalisation: consensus criteria, Jak/Bondi comprehensive criteria, and LCA with information criteria.

signalling.question: Were valid methods used for the identification of the condition?
signalling.quote: Clinical diagnosis was determined by the consensus of at least two clinicians using all available clinical information, including demographics, comprehensive neuropsychological data, functional status, medical and psychiatric history, and neuroimaging. ... Participants were classified as having MCI if they had an impaired score, defined as > 1 SD below the normative mean, on two or more measures within a cognitive domain.

domains.domain: Item 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.rationale: All participants took the same battery, with the same demographically adjusted z-scores feeding every method. Inter-rater reliability of the consensus is not reported. LCA class selection used partly theoretical judgement. The actuarial operationalisation (14 tests in six domains) is broader than earlier applications, which the authors note raises the actuarial MCI rate.

signalling.question: Was the condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants?
signalling.quote: All participants completed the Uniform Data Set prescribed by the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center and additional cognitive tests. ... For all primary analyses, raw scores were converted to z-scores adjusted for age, education, and gender

domains.rationale: The proportions are reported over the full classified sample, and agreement is assessed with kappa and chi-squared tests. No confidence intervals are reported for the rates.

signalling.question: Was there appropriate statistical analysis?
signalling.quote: Differences in race/ethnicity by diagnostic category were examined using Pearson’s chi-squared test. Agreement of MCI diagnostic methods was examined using chi-squared tests and kappa statistics.

domains.domain: Item 9. Response rate adequate or managed
domains.rationale: The paper does not report how many Clinical Core participants were screened, or how many were excluded for incomplete test data or other diagnoses.

signalling.question: Was the response rate adequate, and if not, was the low response rate managed appropriately?
signalling.quote: Searched for the number of Clinical Core participants screened or excluded (incomplete data, other diagnoses) before the analytic sample of 354. None is reported.

applicability.concern: high for absolute prevalence, low for within-sample comparison
applicability.rationale: A highly educated memory-centre research cohort ('The sample was highly educated overall', p. 7). The rates show how the definitions diverge in the same people and are not population prevalence.
The actuarial criteria used more tests and domains than prior applications (p. 12), which inflates actuarial MCI rates relative to other implementations.

overall: Some concerns (JBI prevalence: items 1 and 2 No; items 3 and 9 Unclear; items 4 to 8 Yes)
overall_rationale: Under the review's rule, 'high' is triggered only by No on valid identification or on analysis, and both are Yes here. The No answers concern the sampling frame and method, a non-representative clinic cohort defined partly by consensus diagnosis, and the Unclear answers concern sample size and response. That gives some concerns. The sampling weakness limits the absolute rates much more than the within-sample contrast between definitions that the review draws on.
